entry.title: Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop (18 minute read)
entry.content:
Folding routers, planners, and domain specialists into a single agent loop can reduce lossy handoffs, cost, and latency when skills and tool search load context on demand. Anthropic describes migration patterns and evaluations for deciding which boundaries to remove. Separate agents still help with independent parallel work, verification, permission boundaries, and measurable context overload.

entry.title: Anthropic builds its own source control system (12 minute read)
entry.content:
Anthropic replaced Git in its monorepo with Scion as daily merges grew from about 2,500 to more than 30,000 and CI reached 25 million checkouts a day. Its Rust client and server store changesets in Spanner and blobs in Google Cloud Storage, with a separate review system replacing GitHub's workflow.

entry.title: We Built an AI Agent to Investigate Production Issues (10 minute read)
entry.content:
Stream's incident agent gathers logs, metrics, database results, and code references, then has a fresh session challenge its conclusions before posting findings. Read-only tools, isolated credentials, restricted networking, and output filters enforce its limits outside the prompt. Engineers approve every fix, while 22 evaluation cases test real incidents and past mistakes.

entry.title: Docker is weird (3 minute read)
entry.content:
Building a container runtime exposes Docker as a collection of Linux mechanisms, including namespaces, cgroups, and filesystem isolation around ordinary processes. This walkthrough explains why Go's multithreaded runtime complicates container setup and why rootless networking often requires extra work in userspace.

entry.title: Speeding up code review with small-change (5 minute read)
entry.content:

Eligibility depends on a CI-controlled check covering change size, service experience, scope, and automated review findings, with shared libraries and sensitive paths excluded. Errors are treated as failures to improve in the verification system.

entry.title: Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption? (11 minute read)
entry.content:
AI adoption needs changes to incentives, working practices, and support alongside software licenses. Staff need role-specific training, time to experiment, and a reason to share in productivity gains without fearing punishment for mistakes. Shadow AI can reveal gaps in official tools that blanket restrictions only push out of sight.

entry.title: How we cut GitLab Duo Code Review's cost by 98% (11 minute read)
entry.content:

Compaction made oversized reviews fit the deployment's context window, removing expensive fallbacks to Sonnet.

entry.title: What the heck is the Public Suffix List? (21 minute read)
entry.content:
The Public Suffix List records the boundaries browsers and password managers need to distinguish independently controlled sites on shared domains. Its rules prevent cookies and saved credentials from crossing tenant boundaries, but growing demand leaves volunteers reviewing increasingly complex submissions. The article explains why DNS has not replaced the list and why using it for unrelated controls can create problems.

entry.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale (15 minute read)
entry.content:
Claude produced machine-checked proofs for 239 fuzz-test entry points across 123 open-source libraries, turning existing tests into specifications over compiled RISC-V code. The guarantees cover inputs below 64 MB under a single-threaded Linux model with fixed memory limits, so they establish specific security properties rather than complete program correctness.

entry.content:

entry.title: On Alignment That Looks Wrong (7 minute read)
entry.content:
Flexbox can center an SVG perfectly while the drawing inside still looks misplaced. Inspecting the viewport, correcting uneven viewBox space, and adjusting visual weight at the asset or component level produces better results than scattering pixel nudges across consumers. Play buttons, circle sizing, and hanging punctuation show why mathematical alignment and optical balance differ.

entry.content:

Sandboxing and reuse remain possible defenses, but each has limitations.

entry.title: Making a website AI friendly: what the bots actually fetched from mine (17 minute read)
entry.content:
An analysis of 18 days of traffic to one personal site found that verified crawlers mostly fetched ordinary pages, robots.txt, and the sitemap. Markdown copies attracted verified crawlers within a day, while llms.txt saw no verified training or search crawler requests, suggesting that basic HTML and measured traffic matter more than adding every proposed discovery file.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-10-20 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: The generic circular dependency problem (15 minute read)
entry.content:
Generic services become coupled to their consumers when shared types or domain logic pull application knowledge back into analytics, email, or authorization modules. Domain wrappers, locally owned handlers, smaller contracts, and plugin registration can break those cycles, while extracting a shared type package may only hide the conceptual coupling.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-10-20 · Articles & Tutorials

entry.title: Writing is no longer proof of work (6 minute read)
entry.content:
Organizations often use reports and templates as evidence that someone put in effort, followed a process, or understood a topic. LLMs weaken that signal by producing plausible documents without the underlying work, leaving companies to find better evidence and reserve careful writing for actual communication.

The team migrated through 45 pull requests across eight stacks, using vertical slices and before-and-after screenshots, then removed the old patterns so agents would stop copying them.

entry.title: HybridAgent Thinks in Latent Space and Acts in Text (6 minute read)
entry.content:
HybridAgent is a research approach for training AI agents to reason internally using numerical representations instead of writing out every intermediate thought, while still producing text to call tools such as Python or web search and deliver answers. In tests, a 14B Qwen3 model trained this way scored 52.4 on GAIA versus 43.7 for a matched text-only agent, with estimated decoding costs falling from $470 to $176 per million questions.

entry.title: Exploring AWS Lambda Web Functions for building web applications (9 minute read)
entry.content:

In a sample run of 300 streaming requests with up to 200 open at once, five environments consumed 4.75 seconds of CPU. Billing covers active CPU, memory, and requests, so waiting on a database or API uses little CPU but still incurs other charges.

entry.content:

From TLDR Dev · 2026-10-19 · Opinions & Advice

entry.title: What Requirements Don't You Have? (7 minute read)
entry.content:
Elegant systems often gain simplicity and scale by accepting limits on freshness, coordination, or flexibility. Coding agents tend to invent extra requirements, so explicitly stating which compromises are acceptable can prevent unnecessary locks, checks, and layers of abstraction.

From TLDR Dev · 2026-10-19 · Opinions & Advice

entry.title: Does Ruby on Rails Still Make Sense? (8 minute read)
entry.content:
Frameworks remain useful when agents write the code because they supply structure, shared maintenance, and familiar abstractions. Rewriting an application in a faster language can change behavior that users rely on, making targeted optimization and dependency updates a more practical starting point. Familiar code also makes it easier to review the decisions an agent makes.

Its long-context answers still missed or invented dependencies, showing why the results need to be read beyond the headline scores.

entry.title: Building a computer that can pause and resume in milliseconds: Inside the MicroVM architecture behind Managed Agents (20 minute read)

entry.title: A Single POST Freezes Any Next.js Server (3 minute read)
entry.content:
A React Server Components flaw let an attacker force quadratic work while React rebuilt FormData for a server action, allowing a roughly 900 KB request to trigger 100 million string checks and block a Node.js event loop. The issue affects vulnerable React 19.0 to 19.2 releases and is fixed in 19.0.6, 19.1.7, and 19.2.6.
